bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Balance-sheet claim for FY26: "Despite significant investments in manufacturing facilities and expansion initiatives, Advait has maintained a strong balance sheet with D/E of only 0.3x and Net Worth of INR 291 Cr. in FY26."
- Returns framing: "The Company has consistently maintained ROCE above 20%, reaching 28.0% in FY26. Even after the strategic capital raise in FY25, ROE remained at 18.6%, reflecting disciplined capital deployment."
- Growth is capex- and partnership-funded rather than distribution-oriented; the MD cites "a disciplined capital allocation strategy" but the deck states no dividend or buyback policy.
- Strategy is to establish presence before committing capacity: "Leveraging technology partnerships and anchor project execution to establish market presence before scaling capacity", and in Phase I "building early customer relationships and domain credibility before committing capital".
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Qualification moat: utility procurement awards contracts on demonstrated execution, and Advait has accumulated over 10 years of pre-qualification credentials that a well-funded competitor cannot purchase - validated by every utility board approval, ahead-of-schedule delivery and repeat order
- Extreme-terrain execution record: 250 km of OPGW stringing across Leh and Ladakh above 12,500 feet in minus fifteen degrees Celsius, and more than 25,000 km of live-line installations across 15 or more Indian states
- Technology moat: exclusive Indian manufacturing and commercialisation rights for advanced alkaline electrolyser technology, plus a technology transfer agreement with a Norwegian provider for PEM fuel cells (partners named as Jiangsu Guofuhee for electrolysers and AVL and TECO for fuel cells)
- First indigenous ERS manufacturer in India across the full 33 kV to 800 kV voltage spectrum, at a time when the Central Electricity Authority mandates ERS deployment by circuit-kilometre density
- Approximately 50% domestic market share in stringing tools, with more than 140 types offered
- Integrated group model: BESS and electrolysers manufactured in-house are deployed on the Company's own IPP and green hydrogen projects and installed by its own EPC teams, capturing manufacturing margin plus EPC margin plus asset-ownership yield
- Dedicated subsidiary structure gives each vertical its own capital structure, leadership and P&L accountability, so each can attract the investor class suited to its risk profile - project-level debt for IPP, green bonds for storage, technology equity for electrolysers
- Reference-asset credentials in emerging markets: India's first operational green hydrogen microgrid (THDC India), a 1 MW green hydrogen generation project at Bharuch, and 75 MW solar commissioned at Khavda
- Repeat business from utilities - successive orders each increasing in value and technical complexity - lowering customer acquisition cost and improving margin predictability
- NABL-certified in-house testing laboratory giving independent test rigour to OPGW, ERS and stringing tools before field despatch
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- No separate Risk Management Committee at board level — The Company states it 'does not have a separate Risk Management Committee', with risk responsibilities instead embedded across functions and overseen by senior management, and the Board informed through regular reviews. For a group scaling revenue and adding capital-intensive verticals at this pace, oversight without a dedicated board committee is a structural governance gap.
- Execution and commissioning risk on the Gangad manufacturing complex — The next phase of growth depends on a single large integrated complex - a 150,000 square metre site with HTLS, BESS, electrolyser and fuel cell lines - whose Phase 1 is targeted for Q4 FY27 with full commercialisation by mid-2028. The Directors' Report separately states the same facility is expected to be operational by September 2026; the unreconciled dates within the same annual report underline timeline uncertainty, and slippage would delay the capacity the strategy is built on.
- Building capacity ahead of demand — The Company states the facility's capacity 'has been planned for where India's energy requirements are expected to be by 2030 and beyond, well ahead of today's demand levels', and that being an early mover 'demands conviction, continuous investment and the willingness to build capabilities ahead of market maturity'. If clean-energy demand matures more slowly than assumed, the investment carries utilisation and return risk.
- Dependence on external technology licences and partners — The electrolyser and fuel cell verticals rest on technology transfer and licensing arrangements with global players (named in the AR as Jiangsu Guofuhee for electrolysers and AVL and TECO for fuel cells), and Power Conversion Systems are sourced through strategic partners. The Group's clean-energy capability is therefore contingent on these relationships and on the phased localisation roadmap actually delivering in-house capability.
- Concentration on government, utility and DISCOM customers — The order book is dominated by central and state utilities and DISCOM schemes - PGCIL, GETCO, PGVCL, UGVCL, DGVCL, and RDSS/System Improvement Schemes - so revenue depends heavily on government capital allocation and procurement cycles. Management itself flags private-sector demand as only now 'emerging as a distinct stream'.
- Externally driven risk factors the Board monitors continuously — The Board's risk framework names changes in market dynamics, regulatory developments, cybersecurity threats, supply chain disruptions and macroeconomic conditions as the internal and external factors under ongoing evaluation - a standing exposure set for a business dependent on imported technology inputs and long-cycle infrastructure contracts.
- Contingent exposure through guarantees and surety bonds — Bank guarantees, letters of credit, bills and corporate guarantees amount to Rs 30,042 lakh, including a Rs 2,000 lakh corporate guarantee issued in favour of ICICI Bank on behalf of a subsidiary, and surety bonds outstanding at 31 March 2026 of Rs 2,253.11 lakh against nil a year earlier. These off-balance-sheet obligations scale with the contracting book, though management does not expect any material cash outflow.
- Loss-making associate and early-stage subsidiaries — The associate TG Advait India Private Limited, held at 33.50%, reported a loss for the year, and the newly incorporated wholly-owned tools subsidiary is also loss-making. The multi-subsidiary structure that gives each vertical independent P&L accountability also means several verticals are pre-profit while the listed transmission business funds the transition.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Transform from a power-infrastructure solutions provider into an integrated, diversified energy-transition platform, broadening from transmission and distribution into BESS, green hydrogen, electrolysers, fuel-cell technologies, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing.
- Operate each energy-transition vertical through a dedicated subsidiary with its own capital structure, leadership and P&L accountability, so each can attract the investor class suited to its risk profile - project-level debt for the IPP platform, green bonds for storage, technology-focused equity for the electrolyser business.
- Partner with globally recognised technology leaders and combine their proven expertise with Indian manufacturing - exclusive Indian rights for advanced alkaline electrolyser technology and a technology-transfer agreement with a Norwegian provider for PEM fuel cells - then progressively localise rather than merely assemble imported technology.
- Build an integrated value chain in which electrolysers and BESS manufactured in-house are deployed on the Company's own IPP and green hydrogen assets and installed by its own EPC teams, capturing manufacturing, EPC and asset-ownership economics.
- Consolidate PTS and NRE manufacturing into a single integrated Gangad complex, sized for where India's energy requirements are expected to be by 2030 and beyond rather than for today's demand.
- Develop renewable assets through the AURA independent power production platform, anchored on long-term contracted BESS concessions.
- Pursue solar EPC with deliberate selectivity - accepting projects that meet return thresholds and declining those that do not, prioritising margin discipline over volume.
- Extend transmission credentials into international markets, reactivating the Africa and Middle East EPC presence built between 2009 and 2017 for technology-led engagements and pursuing qualification-level work in South-East Asia, Africa and Central Asia.
- Build ACARA, the carbon advisory and climate-services vertical, as a pillar of an integrated energy-transition and climate-solutions platform combining climate intelligence, environmental attributes and carbon-market capabilities.
- Run a phased roadmap for localisation, manufacturing scale-up and automation across the emerging PEM fuel cell and AEM electrolyser platform to build proprietary execution capabilities.
- Strengthen a centralised procurement ecosystem to standardise sourcing, deepen vendor partnerships and improve operational efficiency across the Group.
- Continue to pursue expansion in the domestic market to achieve sustained and profitable growth.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The centrepiece of Advait's expansion is the Gangad integrated manufacturing complex, being built on a 150,000 square metre plot along the Ahmedabad-Dholera six-lane expressway with a built footprint of over 4 lakh sq. ft. Described as one campus with six manufacturing lines, it consolidates PTS and NRE manufacturing under a single roof: Battery Energy Storage assembly for C&I and grid utility products, electrolyser production lines, Emergency Restoration System manufacturing for the full voltage spectrum, upcoming HTLS conductor manufacturing sized for India's re-conductoring programme, stringing tools production at twice the current capacity, and early-stage fuel cell manufacturing capability through technology partnerships. Planned annual capacities are HTLS conductors 12,000 km, BESS manufacturing 2.5 GWh, AWE electrolyser 300 MW, plus a PEM fuel cell facility. The sequencing was deliberate: before committing to the Gangad scale-up the Company commissioned a 30 MW electrolyser assembly plant at its existing Ahmedabad (Kadi) facility in March 2026 as a working proof of concept. Phase 1 of Gangad is on track for commissioning by Q4 FY27, with full commercialisation expected by mid-2028; the Directors' Report separately states the facility is expected to be operational by September 2026, and the corporate-overview panel states 'to be operational in Q4 FY27' - the two dates are stated in different chapters of the same annual report and are not reconciled in the text. The BESS factory at Dholera is targeted for commissioning by Q4 FY27 with 80 to 85% utilisation expected within eighteen months of launch, and an electrolyser Phase 2 target of 100 MW is set for FY27. The facility is deliberately sized for where India's energy requirements are expected to be by 2030 and beyond rather than for today's demand, and is integrated downstream: BESS made at Gangad will be deployed across the Company's own IPP projects, its electrolysers will support its own green hydrogen projects while also serving the external market, and its own EPC teams will install the hardware. On the asset side, two standalone BESS IPP projects have been secured - 50 MW / 100 MWh at Radhanpur and 150 MW / 300 MWh at Junagadh, Gujarat - under 12-year BESPAs with GUVNL. Existing capacity is also being deepened: OPGW manufacturing at Kadi exceeds 8,000 km per year, ERS capacity reaches approximately 350 towers per year with the expansion of the existing facility, and stringing tools capacity is being expanded from approximately Rs 30-40 crore to Rs 80-100 crore annually. No rupee capital-expenditure quantum is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Grid resilience has become a procurement priority: tower failures reached 75 in the first half of FY25 alone, exceeding the 74 recorded in the entire previous year, moving emergency restoration from a contingency budget to a standing line item.
- Regulatory compulsion rather than discretionary spending - the Central Electricity Authority mandates ERS deployment by circuit-kilometre density: one set below 5,000 CKM, two sets for 5,000 to 10,000 CKM, three sets above 10,000 CKM - and Advait is the first domestic manufacturer across the full 33 kV to 800 kV spectrum.
- State distribution companies are scaling EPC budgets, with multiple orders exceeding Rs 100 crore from individual state utilities in a single year signalling a sustained multi-year expansion in distribution infrastructure under National RDSS and System Improvement Schemes.
- Repeat business from trust-based utility relationships - successive orders each increasing in value and technical complexity, and ERS replenishment following first deployment - translating into lower customer acquisition cost and higher margin predictability.
- Private-sector demand has increased significantly over the past year, emerging as a distinct stream that diversifies the customer base beyond utilities.
- Clean energy demand is transitioning from pilot to procurement: a 100 MWh grid-stability project in execution marks the shift from pilot-scale to procurement-scale storage deployment.
- India's largest renewable developers now treat Advait as a credible EPC partner, with multi-megawatt solar commissions at Khavda pre-qualifying the Company for subsequent renewable EPC opportunities.
- Heavy industry decarbonisation is creating a new buyer class - fertiliser and steel are identified as target electrolyser customers facing regulatory pressure to cut process emissions and evaluating green hydrogen as a feedstock substitute; the buyer class driving electrolyser demand at scale is industrial, not utility.
- The BESS revenue architecture spans DC component supply (65-70% of project value) and integration, AC components, and long-term operations and maintenance (30%).
- BESS demand is driven by India's Energy Storage Obligation (ESO) market and increasing Commercial & Industrial segment requirements, addressing the grid-stabilisation imperative from accelerating solar and wind capacity.
- Electrolyser manufacturing is backed by the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme of the Government of India and targets green hydrogen and green ammonia producers and offtakers.
- International demand is maturing from heritage relationships to qualification-level engagement, with exclusive regional technology rights setting the geographic ceiling - the addressable market is the region, not the country.
- Advait's HTLS re-conductoring proposition is supported by the value of upgrading existing corridors in densely populated and urban areas where acquiring land for new power corridors is difficult and expensive.
- Ahead-of-schedule delivery protects margins against inflationary overhead and earns repeat business visible in the order book.
- The order book has grown 159% year-on-year to reach Rs 1,304 crore.
- Power Transmission Solutions carries 64% of the order book; New Renewable Energy carries 36%.
- Rs 90 crore ERS supply order from Power Grid Corporation of India (765 kV and 400 kV), described as the largest ERS contract of its kind in India.
- Rs 463 crore of new orders secured in the DISCOM segment during FY 2025-26 under the RDSS and System Improvement Schemes, including a Rs 208 crore single order from PGVCL.

risks.risk: No separate Risk Management Committee at board level
risks.note: The Company states it 'does not have a separate Risk Management Committee', with risk responsibilities instead embedded across functions and overseen by senior management, and the Board informed through regular reviews. For a group scaling revenue and adding capital-intensive verticals at this pace, oversight without a dedicated board committee is a structural governance gap.

risks.risk: Execution and commissioning risk on the Gangad manufacturing complex
risks.note: The next phase of growth depends on a single large integrated complex - a 150,000 square metre site with HTLS, BESS, electrolyser and fuel cell lines - whose Phase 1 is targeted for Q4 FY27 with full commercialisation by mid-2028. The Directors' Report separately states the same facility is expected to be operational by September 2026; the unreconciled dates within the same annual report underline timeline uncertainty, and slippage would delay the capacity the strategy is built on.

The Company states the facility's capacity 'has been planned for where India's energy requirements are expected to be by 2030 and beyond, well ahead of today's demand levels', and that being an early mover 'demands conviction, continuous investment and the willingness to build capabilities ahead of market maturity'. If clean-energy demand matures more slowly than assumed, the investment carries utilisation and return risk.

risks.risk: Dependence on external technology licences and partners
risks.note: The electrolyser and fuel cell verticals rest on technology transfer and licensing arrangements with global players (named in the AR as Jiangsu Guofuhee for electrolysers and AVL and TECO for fuel cells), and Power Conversion Systems are sourced through strategic partners. The Group's clean-energy capability is therefore contingent on these relationships and on the phased localisation roadmap actually delivering in-house capability.

risks.risk: Concentration on government, utility and DISCOM customers
risks.note: The order book is dominated by central and state utilities and DISCOM schemes - PGCIL, GETCO, PGVCL, UGVCL, DGVCL, and RDSS/System Improvement Schemes - so revenue depends heavily on government capital allocation and procurement cycles. Management itself flags private-sector demand as only now 'emerging as a distinct stream'.

risks.risk: Externally driven risk factors the Board monitors continuously
risks.note: The Board's risk framework names changes in market dynamics, regulatory developments, cybersecurity threats, supply chain disruptions and macroeconomic conditions as the internal and external factors under ongoing evaluation - a standing exposure set for a business dependent on imported technology inputs and long-cycle infrastructure contracts.

risks.risk: Contingent exposure through guarantees and surety bonds
risks.note: Bank guarantees, letters of credit, bills and corporate guarantees amount to Rs 30,042 lakh, including a Rs 2,000 lakh corporate guarantee issued in favour of ICICI Bank on behalf of a subsidiary, and surety bonds outstanding at 31 March 2026 of Rs 2,253.11 lakh against nil a year earlier. These off-balance-sheet obligations scale with the contracting book, though management does not expect any material cash outflow.

The associate TG Advait India Private Limited, held at 33.50%, reported a loss for the year, and the newly incorporated wholly-owned tools subsidiary is also loss-making. The multi-subsidiary structure that gives each vertical independent P&L accountability also means several verticals are pre-profit while the listed transmission business funds the transition.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company manufactures and supplies power transmission and distribution products - OPGW cables, Aluminium Clad Steel (ACS) wires, Emergency Restoration System (ERS) towers across the 33 kV to 800 kV range, HTLS conductors and transmission-line stringing tools - and provides specialised EPC services including live-line OPGW installation, HTLS re-conductoring and turnkey distribution contracts under the RDSS and System Improvement Schemes. Since 2023 it has diversified into new and renewable energy through dedicated subsidiaries covering AEM/alkaline electrolysers, battery energy storage systems, PEM fuel cells, solar EPC and carbon advisory. An asset-ownership platform (AURA) is being built to own power-generating assets, so that self-manufactured electrolysers and BESS can be deployed on the Company's own IPP projects. Customers are principally state and central utilities (PGCIL, GETCO, PGVCL, UGVCL, DGVCL), renewable developers and, increasingly, private-sector and international buyers.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Grid resilience has become a procurement priority: tower failures reached 75 in the first half of FY25 alone, exceeding the 74 recorded in the entire previous year, moving emergency restoration from a contingency budget to a standing line item.
- Regulatory compulsion rather than discretionary spending - the Central Electricity Authority mandates ERS deployment by circuit-kilometre density: one set below 5,000 CKM, two sets for 5,000 to 10,000 CKM, three sets above 10,000 CKM - and Advait is the first domestic manufacturer across the full 33 kV to 800 kV spectrum.
- State distribution companies are scaling EPC budgets, with multiple orders exceeding Rs 100 crore from individual state utilities in a single year signalling a sustained multi-year expansion in distribution infrastructure under National RDSS and System Improvement Schemes.
- Repeat business from trust-based utility relationships - successive orders each increasing in value and technical complexity, and ERS replenishment following first deployment - translating into lower customer acquisition cost and higher margin predictability.
- Private-sector demand has increased significantly over the past year, emerging as a distinct stream that diversifies the customer base beyond utilities.
- Clean energy demand is transitioning from pilot to procurement: a 100 MWh grid-stability project in execution marks the shift from pilot-scale to procurement-scale storage deployment.
- India's largest renewable developers now treat Advait as a credible EPC partner, with multi-megawatt solar commissions at Khavda pre-qualifying the Company for subsequent renewable EPC opportunities.
- Heavy industry decarbonisation is creating a new buyer class - fertiliser and steel are identified as target electrolyser customers facing regulatory pressure to cut process emissions and evaluating green hydrogen as a feedstock substitute; the buyer class driving electrolyser demand at scale is industrial, not utility.
- The BESS revenue architecture spans DC component supply (65-70% of project value) and integration, AC components, and long-term operations and maintenance (30%).
- BESS demand is driven by India's Energy Storage Obligation (ESO) market and increasing Commercial & Industrial segment requirements, addressing the grid-stabilisation imperative from accelerating solar and wind capacity.
- Electrolyser manufacturing is backed by the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme of the Government of India and targets green hydrogen and green ammonia producers and offtakers.
- International demand is maturing from heritage relationships to qualification-level engagement, with exclusive regional technology rights setting the geographic ceiling - the addressable market is the region, not the country.
- Advait's HTLS re-conductoring proposition is supported by the value of upgrading existing corridors in densely populated and urban areas where acquiring land for new power corridors is difficult and expensive.
- Ahead-of-schedule delivery protects margins against inflationary overhead and earns repeat business visible in the order book.
- The order book has grown 159% year-on-year to reach Rs 1,304 crore.
- Power Transmission Solutions carries 64% of the order book; New Renewable Energy carries 36%.
- Rs 90 crore ERS supply order from Power Grid Corporation of India (765 kV and 400 kV), described as the largest ERS contract of its kind in India.
- Rs 463 crore of new orders secured in the DISCOM segment during FY 2025-26 under the RDSS and System Improvement Schemes, including a Rs 208 crore single order from PGVCL.
- Rs 61 crore re-conductoring order from GETCO, adding to repeated HTLS orders from the same utility.
- Rs 86 crore of orders secured from PGCIL for OPGW Live-Line projects.
- Rs 3.33 crore order from PowerGrid for Tower Erection Cranes under its Vendor Development initiative, marking entry into a new product category.
- Stringing tools recorded their highest-ever backlog of around Rs 22 crore in FY26.
- Each clean-energy subsidiary is developing its own order book, with the potential to compound independently.
- OPGW live-line installation and service projects secured in Malaysia; a 500-kilometre OPGW Expression of Interest submitted in Ethiopia; pipeline development underway in Kazakhstan.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The centrepiece of Advait's expansion is the Gangad integrated manufacturing complex, being built on a 150,000 square metre plot along the Ahmedabad-Dholera six-lane expressway with a built footprint of over 4 lakh sq. ft. Described as one campus with six manufacturing lines, it consolidates PTS and NRE manufacturing under a single roof: Battery Energy Storage assembly for C&I and grid utility products, electrolyser production lines, Emergency Restoration System manufacturing for the full voltage spectrum, upcoming HTLS conductor manufacturing sized for India's re-conductoring programme, stringing tools production at twice the current capacity, and early-stage fuel cell manufacturing capability through technology partnerships. Planned annual capacities are HTLS conductors 12,000 km, BESS manufacturing 2.5 GWh, AWE electrolyser 300 MW, plus a PEM fuel cell facility. The sequencing was deliberate: before committing to the Gangad scale-up the Company commissioned a 30 MW electrolyser assembly plant at its existing Ahmedabad (Kadi) facility in March 2026 as a working proof of concept. Phase 1 of Gangad is on track for commissioning by Q4 FY27, with full commercialisation expected by mid-2028; the Directors' Report separately states the facility is expected to be operational by September 2026, and the corporate-overview panel states 'to be operational in Q4 FY27' - the two dates are stated in different chapters of the same annual report and are not reconciled in the text. The BESS factory at Dholera is targeted for commissioning by Q4 FY27 with 80 to 85% utilisation expected within eighteen months of launch, and an electrolyser Phase 2 target of 100 MW is set for FY27. The facility is deliberately sized for where India's energy requirements are expected to be by 2030 and beyond rather than for today's demand, and is integrated downstream: BESS made at Gangad will be deployed across the Company's own IPP projects, its electrolysers will support its own green hydrogen projects while also serving the external market, and its own EPC teams will install the hardware. On the asset side, two standalone BESS IPP projects have been secured - 50 MW / 100 MWh at Radhanpur and 150 MW / 300 MWh at Junagadh, Gujarat - under 12-year BESPAs with GUVNL. Existing capacity is also being deepened: OPGW manufacturing at Kadi exceeds 8,000 km per year, ERS capacity reaches approximately 350 towers per year with the expansion of the existing facility, and stringing tools capacity is being expanded from approximately Rs 30-40 crore to Rs 80-100 crore annually. No rupee capital-expenditure quantum is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Qualification moat: utility procurement awards contracts on demonstrated execution, and Advait has accumulated over 10 years of pre-qualification credentials that a well-funded competitor cannot purchase - validated by every utility board approval, ahead-of-schedule delivery and repeat order
- Extreme-terrain execution record: 250 km of OPGW stringing across Leh and Ladakh above 12,500 feet in minus fifteen degrees Celsius, and more than 25,000 km of live-line installations across 15 or more Indian states
- Technology moat: exclusive Indian manufacturing and commercialisation rights for advanced alkaline electrolyser technology, plus a technology transfer agreement with a Norwegian provider for PEM fuel cells (partners named as Jiangsu Guofuhee for electrolysers and AVL and TECO for fuel cells)
- First indigenous ERS manufacturer in India across the full 33 kV to 800 kV voltage spectrum, at a time when the Central Electricity Authority mandates ERS deployment by circuit-kilometre density
- Approximately 50% domestic market share in stringing tools, with more than 140 types offered
- Integrated group model: BESS and electrolysers manufactured in-house are deployed on the Company's own IPP and green hydrogen projects and installed by its own EPC teams, capturing manufacturing margin plus EPC margin plus asset-ownership yield
- Dedicated subsidiary structure gives each vertical its own capital structure, leadership and P&L accountability, so each can attract the investor class suited to its risk profile - project-level debt for IPP, green bonds for storage, technology equity for electrolysers
- Reference-asset credentials in emerging markets: India's first operational green hydrogen microgrid (THDC India), a 1 MW green hydrogen generation project at Bharuch, and 75 MW solar commissioned at Khavda
- Repeat business from utilities - successive orders each increasing in value and technical complexity - lowering customer acquisition cost and improving margin predictability
- NABL-certified in-house testing laboratory giving independent test rigour to OPGW, ERS and stringing tools before field despatch
